items.title: 13.10.2 Reaction with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide

source_refs.note: Topic 13.10.2, printed page 300. The unbalanced printed equation is balanced and noted.

blocks.text: With hot aqueous sodium hydroxide chlorine forms sodium chloride and sodium chlorate(V), NaClO3, another disproportionation: 3Cl2(g) + 6NaOH(aq) gives 5NaCl(aq) + NaClO3(aq) + 3H2O(l) (the print omits the coefficient 5). Chlorine is 0 in Cl2, -1 in NaCl and +5 in NaClO3: it is oxidised from 0 to +5 in NaClO3 and reduced from 0 to -1 in NaCl. The reaction shows how temperature influences the products and the versatility of chlorine in redox reactions.

blocks.prompt: Write balanced equations for chlorine with cold dilute and with hot concentrated NaOH, and use oxidation states to explain why both are disproportionations (exercise Q.2o, p).
blocks.explanation: Cold: Cl2 + 2NaOH gives NaCl + NaClO + H2O; Cl goes 0 to -1 and 0 to +1. Hot: 3Cl2 + 6NaOH gives 5NaCl + NaClO3 + 3H2O; Cl goes 0 to -1 (five atoms) and 0 to +5 (one atom, which loses the five electrons the others gain). In each case chlorine alone is both oxidised and reduced, so both are disproportionations; the hotter, stronger alkali pushes the oxidation further to chlorate(V).

items: Hot NaOH: 3Cl2 + 6NaOH gives 5NaCl + NaClO3 + 3H2O; Cl 0 to -1 (reduced) and 0 to +5 (oxidised); temperature decides chlorate(I) or chlorate(V).
